newsitem.title: UK: Dlr ends firm but off peaks in Europe after G7.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends firm but off peaks in Europe after G7.

text.p: The dollar closed firmer but off highs as dealers netted short-term profits from its rise triggered by a benign forex statement from Group of Seven (G7) finance ministers at the weekend.
Traders said a slight retreat was natural after the dollar's rally overnight to a fresh 37-month high against the mark and to near its 55-month peak against the yen.

"The outcome of this G7 meeting should be read as an indication that the G7 is still fairly content with a strong dollar though wary of overshooting in the future," said Joe Prendergast, currency strategist at Merrill Lynch in London.

In a communique after Sunday's meeting in Washington, the finance ministers said major currency misalignments had been corrected, and excessive volatility and deviations from fundamentals were undesirable.

The contents of the statement were mostly what the market had expected, with analysts saying it lacked aggressiveness. The market is likely to test central banks' resolve on intervention by bidding the dollar up gradually as fundamentals remain on the favourable side for the U.S. currency.
"The G7 meeting has left the foreign exchange market in the mood to test official resolve to maintain stable exchange rates," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking.
The dollar was at 1.7288/98 marks at 1450 GMT, down from its overnight high of 1.7395, according to Bank of Japan data, but still up from 1.7241/51 in late European trade on Friday.
It was at 126.60/70 yen, off a peak of 127.10 hit overnight but up from 125.90/00 late here on Friday.
Analysts agreed the authorities were likely to tolerate a rise in the dollar as long as it was slow, citing a comment made by Bank of England governor Eddie George after the meeting.
George said the G7 felt the currency environment was "in pretty good shape", and that no need had been expressed at the meeting for an action plan to deal with future currency moves.
Key focus for the dollar is the non-farm payrolls data on Friday. The currency is likely to be given a filip if the jobs data is strong, analysts said.
The market did not see the G7's reference to trade imbalances as a major threat, adding that it only suggested there was some concern among leading nations.
"We're not at the stage yet where we can see the G7 is desperately worried about trade imbalances," said Stephen Hannah, director of research at IBJ International here.
"They're trying to avoid a situation in which trade imbalances become a big problem, which can occur if we see further strong rises in the dollar," Hannah said.

The Canadian dollar weakened after Prime Minister Jean Chretien called a June 2 election on Sunday, 17 months before it was due. The Canadian dollar was at C$1.3991/96 dollar against C$1.3965/70 late Friday.

Traders said the Canadian election is unlikely to have a dramatic near-term impact on the currency market because the ruling Liberal Party is such a clear front-runner and investors remain focused on the U.S. rate situation.
